notes.definition: Background radiation is the ionising radiation that is around us all of the time, from natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays and from man-made sources such as fallout from nuclear weapons testing and nuclear accidents.
explanation: Background radiation is around us all of the time. Most of it comes from natural sources. Some rocks, such as granite, contain radioactive isotopes of uranium, thorium and potassium. The uranium decays to radon, a radioactive gas that seeps out of the ground and can collect in buildings; in the UK radon is the largest single source of background radiation. Cosmic rays from space (from the Sun and beyond) also reach the Earth. Small amounts of radioactive isotopes are also in our food and drink, and therefore in our bodies.

Some background radiation comes from man-made sources. These include fallout from nuclear weapons testing carried out in the past, and radioactive material released in nuclear accidents such as Chernobyl and Fukushima. Medical procedures such as X-rays and CT scans also add to the dose of an average person.

The level of background radiation and the radiation dose a person receives depend on their location and occupation. People living in areas with granite rocks, such as parts of Cornwall and Scotland, receive a higher dose from radon and gamma rays from the ground. Aircrew and frequent flyers receive more cosmic radiation, because there is less atmosphere above them to absorb it. Workers in nuclear power stations, hospitals and some mines may receive a higher dose from their jobs.

Radiation dose measures the risk of harm from the radiation that a person's body absorbs. It is measured in sieverts (Sv). One sievert is a large dose, so doses are usually given in millisieverts (mSv): 1000 mSv = 1 Sv. A typical person in the UK receives about 2 to 3 mSv per year from background radiation.

When measuring the count rate from a radioactive source in the laboratory, background radiation is always detected too. Scientists measure the background count rate with no source present, then subtract it from each reading, to find the count rate due to the source alone.
keyFacts: Background radiation is around us all of the time.
Natural sources include rocks (and the radon gas they release) and cosmic rays from space.
Man-made sources include fallout from nuclear weapons testing and nuclear accidents.
Radon gas is the biggest single source of background radiation in the UK.
Background radiation level and dose depend on location and occupation.
Radiation dose is measured in sieverts (Sv).
A typical UK annual background dose is about 2 to 3 mSv.
Subtract the background count rate from measured count rates to find the source's count rate.

keyTerms.definition: Ionising radiation that is present around us all of the time, from natural and man-made sources.
High-energy radiation from space that reaches the Earth's atmosphere and surface.
A radioactive gas produced in the decay of uranium in rocks; it can build up in buildings.
Radioactive material spread through the atmosphere after nuclear weapons tests or nuclear accidents.
A measure of the risk of harm from the radiation absorbed by the body, measured in sieverts (Sv).
The unit of radiation dose; 1 Sv = 1000 mSv.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think most background radiation comes from nuclear power stations.
misconceptions.right: In fact most comes from natural sources such as radon from rocks and cosmic rays. Nuclear power contributes a tiny fraction.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think background radiation can be switched off or removed in an experiment.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is always present, so it must be measured and subtracted from readings.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think everyone receives the same background dose.
misconceptions.right: In fact dose depends on where you live (e.g. granite areas) and your job (e.g. aircrew).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think 1 mSv is bigger than 1 Sv.
misconceptions.right: In fact milli means one thousandth: 1 mSv = 0.001 Sv.

realWorld: Homes in high-radon areas can be fitted with underfloor fans and sealed floors to stop radon building up indoors.
Airline crew are classed as radiation workers in some countries and their cosmic ray doses are monitored.
Radioactive fallout from 1950s and 1960s weapons tests can still be detected in soils and in tree rings.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Physics (8463) only. It is not assessed in Combined Science Trilogy (8464). Students do not need to recall the unit of radiation dose (the sievert), but must be able to use it and convert between Sv and mSv.
examTips: Give named examples of sources: natural (rocks, radon, cosmic rays) and man-made (weapons test fallout, nuclear accidents).
When explaining a different dose, link it clearly to location (e.g. granite rocks) or occupation (e.g. aircrew, radiographers).
To convert Sv to mSv multiply by 1000; mSv to Sv divide by 1000.
In practical questions, always subtract background count rate before using the data.
summary: Natural sources: rocks (radon) and cosmic rays; man-made: weapons fallout and nuclear accidents.
Dose depends on location and occupation.
Radiation dose is measured in sieverts; 1000 mSv = 1 Sv.
Subtract background from measured count rates.

questions.question: Why do airline pilots receive a higher background radiation dose than most people?
options: They spend more time near radon
There is less atmosphere above them to absorb cosmic rays
markScheme: 1 mark: There is less atmosphere above them to absorb cosmic rays
questions.explanation: At high altitude there is less air to absorb cosmic rays, so pilots receive more cosmic radiation.

questions.question: How many millisieverts are there in 2.5 Sv?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2500 mSv
questions.explanation: Multiply by 1000: 2.5 × 1000 = 2500 mSv.

questions.question: A student measures count rates from a source. Why must the background count rate be measured?
options: To find the half-life of the background
To make the source more active
So it can be subtracted to find the count rate from the source alone
markScheme: 1 mark: So it can be subtracted to find the count rate from the source alone
questions.explanation: Background is always detected too, so it is subtracted to leave only the source's contribution.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the results of an investigation using a detector.
Calculate the count rate due to the source.
markScheme: 1 mark: measured count rate = 1500 ÷ 5 = 300 counts/min
1 mark: background = 120 ÷ 4 = 30 counts/min

questions.question: State what is meant by background radiation.
acceptedAnswers: radiation around us all the time
markScheme: 1 mark: radiation that is around us all of the time (from natural and man-made sources)
questions.explanation: Background radiation is always present, wherever you are.

questions.question: Name two natural sources of background radiation.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: rocks/ground/buildings; radon gas; cosmic rays; food and drink
questions.explanation: Rocks and cosmic rays are the ones named in the specification.

questions.question: Give two man-made sources of background radiation.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: fallout from nuclear weapons testing; nuclear accidents (e.g. Chernobyl); medical procedures
questions.explanation: Weapons fallout and nuclear accidents are the key examples.

questions.question: Explain why people living in some parts of Cornwall receive a higher background radiation dose than people in most other parts of the UK.
markScheme: 1 mark: the rocks there (granite) contain radioactive uranium
1 mark: which produces radon gas that builds up in homes / gives off more radiation
questions.explanation: Location affects dose because of the local geology.

questions.question: Suggest two jobs that may lead to a higher radiation dose than average, and give a reason for each.
markScheme: 1 mark: pilot/aircrew, more cosmic rays at high altitude
1 mark: radiographer/nuclear worker/miner, works near sources/X-rays or radon underground
questions.explanation: Each job must be linked to a source of radiation.

questions.question: Explain why radon gas in homes is a health concern even though it comes from a natural source.
markScheme: 1 mark: radon is breathed in so the radioactive material is inside the lungs
1 mark: it emits alpha particles, which are strongly ionising and damage lung cells (increasing cancer risk)
questions.explanation: Natural does not mean safe: radon is an internal contamination hazard.

questions.question:
Scientists measure the background count rate three times.
Table 1 shows the results.
Explain why the readings are different and how the scientists should use them.
markScheme: 1 mark: radioactive decay is random, so the number of counts varies
1 mark: calculate the mean (21 counts per minute) and subtract it from the readings
questions.explanation: Repeating and averaging reduces the effect of random variation: (21 + 18 + 24) ÷ 3 = 21.

questions.question: Which statement about background radiation is correct?
options: It is only found near nuclear power stations
It is around us all of the time
markScheme: 1 mark: It is around us all of the time
questions.explanation: Background radiation is always present, from many natural and man-made sources.

questions.question: A person has a background dose of 2.7 mSv per year. In one year she also has two scans of 4 mSv each. What is her total dose for the year?
markScheme: 1 mark: 10.7 mSv
questions.explanation: Total = 2.7 + 2 × 4 = 10.7 mSv. 6.7 mSv counts only one scan.

questions.question: State how many millisieverts (mSv) are equal to one sievert (Sv).
markScheme: 1 mark: 1000
questions.explanation: Milli means one thousandth, so 1000 mSv = 1 Sv.

questions.question: Describe the sources of background radiation and explain why the radiation dose received can be different for different people.
markScheme: Indicative content: natural sources: rocks (granite), radon gas, cosmic rays, food and drink; man-made: fallout from weapons testing, nuclear accidents, medical procedures; dose depends on location, e.g. granite areas have more radon, high altitude more cosmic rays; dose depends on occupation, e.g. pilots, radiographers, nuclear workers, miners.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): natural and man-made sources named, and differences in dose clearly linked to both location and occupation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some sources named or one factor given with little explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Name sources from both categories and link differences to location and occupation with examples.

questions.question:
A family lives in a granite area. The mother is an airline pilot and the father works in a hospital X-ray department. The child is at school all day.
Evaluate which family member is likely to receive the highest annual radiation dose. Refer to sources of background radiation, location, occupation and units of dose in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: all three receive natural background, increased by living in a granite area (radon and gamma from rocks), so all above UK average of about 2 to 3 mSv; the pilot receives extra cosmic radiation at altitude, depending on flying hours; the father works with X-rays but hospital workers are shielded and monitored with dosimeters, so extra dose may be small; the child has only the location effect; pilot is likely highest, as extra cosmic dose can be several mSv per year; doses measured in sieverts, usually mSv (1000 mSv = 1 Sv); conclusion depends on hours flown and precautions; radon indoors depends on time spent at home and ventilation.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a reasoned evaluation comparing all three people, linking location and occupation to specific sources, using dose units correctly and reaching a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): compares at least two people with some correct reasoning about sources.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about sources or doses.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A good evaluation says what is common to all (location) and what is extra (occupation), then reaches a justified conclusion.
